meta.title: India Economic Indicators 2014-2030
meta.author: Dr. Varna Sri Raman
meta.notes: Series are annual unless stated. Observed values run through 2026 and reflect the latest official releases retrieved by 10 October 2026 (MoSPI national accounts with the 2025-26 Provisional Estimate, PLFS Monthly Bulletin August 2026, Union Budget 2026-27, CPI August 2026, World Inequality Lab Working Paper 2024/09). One caveat carries across the whole CPI series: MoSPI replaced the 2012=100 index with a 2024=100 index from the January 2026 print, reweighted on HCES 2023-24, so the 2026 inflation figure is not on the same basis as 2014-2025 (see sources.cpiInflation). All values in the 'economic' block are observed (2014-2026); there is no projected year in this block. The 'forecast' block drives the Economic Trajectory tab: these are scenario projections to 2030, and none of them is a prediction. Every assumption is a choice, and every one is documented. Primer datasets (bigPicture, taxTake, spendSplit, stateReturns, realInflation, external, distribution, structure, chinaDivergence, jobsLesson) are drawn from the 'Reading the Indian Economy' citizen primer (16 June 2026).

sources.gdpGrowth: Real GDP growth, MoSPI national accounts. Year Y is the fiscal year that starts in April of Y (2014 = 2014-15), the same convention as the World Bank series used for 2004-2013. 2014-2022: the latest MoSPI estimates on the 2011-12 base (2017-18 6.8, 2018-19 6.5, 2019-20 3.9, 2020-21 -5.8, 2021-22 9.7, 2022-23 7.6). 2023-2025: the new series on base 2022-23 released on 27 February 2026 (2023-24 7.3 final, 2024-25 7.2 first revised, 2025-26 7.8 provisional); on the old base 2023-24 had been 9.2 and 2024-25 6.5. BASIS BREAK at 2023. 2026 (2026-27) is empty: the first annual estimate is due in January 2027. Quarterly growth for April to June 2026 was 7.8%. The World Bank series for 2004-2013 is on the 2011-12 base.
sources.unemployment: 2015: Labour Bureau, Fifth Annual Employment-Unemployment Survey (2015-16), usual principal status, 5.0. 2014 and 2016 are empty: the Labour Bureau published no survey for 2014-15 or 2016-17, and its 2013-14 survey (4.9) belongs to an earlier year. The Labour Bureau series is a different survey from PLFS. 2017-2025: annual rates on usual status (ps+ss). From 2017 a year is the PLFS survey year that starts in July of it (2017 = 2017-18), through 2023 (2023-24); 2024 and 2025 are MoSPI's calendar-year rates. 2026: the average of the 8 PLFS Monthly Bulletins published for 2026 (January to August 2026: January 5, February 4.9, March 5.1, April 5.2, May 5.5, June 5.5, July 5.1, August 5), all-India, persons 15+, rural + urban. BASIS BREAK: the monthly bulletins report current weekly status (CWS), which counts a person as unemployed on the past week's activity and runs well above usual status. The 2026 value is therefore a different measure from the years before it, and most of the rise from 3.1 per cent in 2025 is the change of measure. On the same weekly measure MoSPI's calendar-year rate for 2025 was 5.3 per cent.
sources.youthUnemployment: MoSPI PLFS, usual status (ps+ss), persons aged 15-29, all-India, rural + urban, from api.mospi.gov.in (retrieved 10 October 2026). 2017-2023 are the PLFS survey years starting in July of the year shown (2017 = 2017-18); 2024 and 2025 are MoSPI's calendar-year rates. 2014-2016 are left empty because PLFS began in 2017-18 and no comparable published figure exists. 2026 is left empty until an annual figure is published: the 2026 monthly bulletins average 15.4% for January to August, but they report current weekly status, which runs well above usual status.
sources.graduateUnemployment: MoSPI PLFS, usual status (ps+ss), persons aged 15 and over with a graduate degree, all-India, rural + urban, from api.mospi.gov.in (retrieved 10 October 2026). 2017-2023 are the PLFS survey years starting in July of the year shown (2017 = 2017-18). MoSPI publishes no figure for graduates for 2014-2016 (before PLFS) or for 2024 onward yet, so those years are left empty.
sources.top1Share: World Inequality Lab: Bharti, Chancel, Piketty and Somanchi (2024), 'Income and Wealth Inequality in India, 1922-2023', WIL Working Paper 2024/09, Statistical Appendix, table of per-adult pre-tax national income shares, 1951-2022. The series ends at 2022 (2022-23); 2023-2026 are empty because no annual figure has been published for them. Top 1% share.
sources.bottom50Share: World Inequality Lab: Bharti, Chancel, Piketty and Somanchi (2024), 'Income and Wealth Inequality in India, 1922-2023', WIL Working Paper 2024/09, Statistical Appendix, table of per-adult pre-tax national income shares, 1951-2022. The series ends at 2022 (2022-23); 2023-2026 are empty because no annual figure has been published for them. Bottom 50% share. The share fell to 13.9 in 2017, rose to 15.5 in 2020 and stood at 15.0 in 2022.
sources.formalEmployment: Derived from MoSPI PLFS published tables (api.mospi.gov.in, retrieved 10 October 2026), usual status (ps+ss), all-India, persons: the share of regular wage/salaried workers among all workers, multiplied by the share of regular wage/salaried employees with any social security benefit (100 minus the published share without any). 2017-18: 22.8% x 50.4% = 11.5; 2018-19: 23.8 x 48.1 = 11.4; 2019-20: 22.9 x 45.8 = 10.5; 2020-21: 21.1 x 46.2 = 9.7; 2021-22: 21.5 x 47.0 = 10.1; 2022-23: 20.9 x 46.1 = 9.6; 2023-24: 21.7 x 46.6 = 10.1. The social security table covers regular wage/salaried employees in the non-agricultural sector; regular wage work in agriculture is about 1% of workers. Years are PLFS survey years starting in July of the year shown. 2014-2016 (before PLFS) and 2024 onward (no annual table yet) are left empty.
sources.informalEmployment: 100 minus formalEmployment, for the years formalEmployment has a value.
sources.pressFreedom: Reporters Without Borders, World Press Freedom Index (annual)
sources.fiscalDeficit: Union Budget documents; central government fiscal deficit as % of GDP, for the fiscal year starting in the year shown (2014 = 2014-15). 2025 is the provisional actual for 2025-26 released by the Controller General of Accounts on 1 June 2026 (Rs 15,19,169 crore, 4.4% of GDP); 2026 is the Budget Estimate for 2026-27 (4.3), from the Union Budget of 1 February 2026.
sources.cpiInflation: MoSPI CPI (Combined), year-on-year, calendar-year averages, the same convention as the World Bank series used for 2004-2013. 2014-2025 on base 2012=100. 2026: the average of the monthly prints published for 2026 (January to August 2026: January 2.74, February 3.21, March 3.4, April 3.48, May 3.93, June 4.38, July 4.45, August 4.82). BASIS BREAK: from the January 2026 print (published 12 Feb 2026) MoSPI moved to a new CPI series on base 2024=100, with weights from HCES 2023-24 and the COICOP 2018 classification, replacing base 2012=100. The 2026 value is on a different basis from the years before it. RBI target band 2-6%.
sources.rupeeUSD: Calendar-year average rupees per US dollar: the mean of the monthly averages in the Federal Reserve's H.10 release (FRED series EXINUS), rounded to the nearest rupee. 2026 is January to September (93.9, shown as 94); 2025 averages 87.2. The record low of 96.8 is the Fed's daily rate for 20 May 2026 (DEXINUS 96.82).
sources.ssi: Constructed: SSI = sum(weight × graded severity) on a 0-10 scale, with persistence; 6 documented suppression streams incl. COVID-mortality undercount and the NSO merger. See data/compute_indices.py
sources.fci: Constructed: mean of six components on a relative 0-1 scale. Four are published fiscal ratios, min-max normalised over the years each is published: the cess and surcharge share of gross tax revenue (15th Finance Commission Table 3.8 for 2011-2018; Union Receipt Budgets for 2019-2026), tax devolution as a share of gross tax revenue (16th Finance Commission Annexure 7.1; Budget at a Glance 2026-27), states' own revenue as a share of their revenue receipts (RBI Handbook 2025-26 Table 94) and non-Finance-Commission grants as a share of Union transfers (16th Finance Commission Annexure 7.1). Two are coded: GST from 2017 and the reform-linked borrowing conditions of 2020-21. Rebuilt from these published figures on 10 October 2026; see data/compute_indices.py
sources.dqi: Constructed: geometric mean of V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index (v2x_libdem) × (Freedom House/100) × ((180-RSF rank)/180) × V-Dem Core Civil Society Index (v2xcs_ccsi); see data/compute_indices.py. The two V-Dem columns are the published series verbatim; earlier approximations that overstated the pre-2014 baseline were corrected on 15 August 2026.
sources.gigWorkers: NITI Aayog, India's Booming Gig and Platform Economy (June 2022), Table 14, gig workers in millions, usual principal and subsidiary status. 2017-2019 are NITI's actual estimates for the PLFS survey years starting in July of the year shown (2017-18 5.3, 2018-19 5.4, 2019-20 6.8). 2020 is NITI's figure for 2020-21 (7.7 million), which the Ministry of Labour cites as the current estimate; NITI's table labels it a projection. Later years are NITI projections (14.3 million for 2025-26, 23.5 million for 2029-30) and are left empty here, as are 2014-2016, for which NITI gives no figure. NITI's 2011-12 estimate is 2.5 million.
sources.ruralIncome: NABARD All India Rural Financial Inclusion Survey (NAFIS), average monthly income of rural households: Rs 8,059 in 2016-17 and Rs 12,698 in 2021-22, a nominal rise of 57.6%. Deflated by MoSPI's CPI-Rural (base 2012=100; fiscal-year averages 132.43 and 164.53, a rise of 24.2%), the real rise is 26.8%, about 4.9% a year. Indexed 2016-17 = 100, so 2016 = 100 and 2021 = 126.8. NAFIS has two rounds only; every other year is left empty. The same survey found the share of rural households with outstanding debt rose from 47.4% to 52%.
sources.femaleLFPR: MoSPI PLFS, labour force participation rate, usual status (ps+ss), women aged 15 and over, all-India, rural + urban, from api.mospi.gov.in (retrieved 10 October 2026). 2017-2023 are the PLFS survey years starting in July of the year shown (2017 = 2017-18); 2024 and 2025 are MoSPI's calendar-year rates. 2014-2016 are left empty because PLFS began in 2017-18, and 2026 until an annual figure is published. PLFS counts a woman who helps without pay in a household enterprise as a worker.
sources.international: V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index (v2x_libdem), latest release (data through 2025; the 2026 column carries the 2025 observation forward) + RSF World Press Freedom Index 2026. Both V-Dem columns are on the SAME index: an earlier version of this table had the 2014 column on the Electoral Democracy Index and the 2026 column on the Liberal Democracy Index, which overstated India's decline. Corrected 15 August 2026.
sources.primer: Reading the Indian Economy: A Citizen's Primer (Varna Sri Raman, 16 June 2026). Figures latest available as of June 2026; several provisional, estimated, or illustrative as noted.
sources.syntheticControl: Grier & Grier (2026), 'Promises, Promises'. Figures are transcribed from the authors' published summary (rgrier88.github.io/modi-promises). Underlying data: V-Dem (governance), Penn World Table 11.0 (income). This is an external study that this project did not produce.

forecast.disclaimer: These are scenario projections, and none of them is a prediction. Each path extends the recent trend of an observed series and then applies an explicit annual adjustment for one of three scenarios. Uncertainty bands widen with the horizon because the further out you look, the more the number depends on the assumption and the less it depends on the economy. Read every projection by asking whose assumption it is and what would break it.

reform.label: Reform push
reform.desc: Statistical independence restored, garment/labour-intensive manufacturing prioritised, fiscal federalism rebalanced, formalisation incentives.

baseline.label: Current trajectory
baseline.desc: Recent-trend continuation: policy mix and institutional direction of 2019-2026 persist.

stress.label: Stress
stress.desc: External shock (oil/rupee), weak monsoon, continued informalisation and statistical opacity.

indicators.label: GDP growth
indicators.drivers: Post-COVID base-effect rebounds are fading; the level itself is contested after the 2015 MCA21 revision.
indicators.breaks: An external oil/rupee shock, a weak monsoon, or investment that keeps growing output without jobs or consumption.

indicators.label: Formal employment share
indicators.drivers: On PLFS, coverage fell from 11.5% in 2017-18 to 9.6% in 2022-23 and was 10.1% in 2023-24. Capital-intensive PLI adds output without adding much payroll.
indicators.breaks: A pivot to labour-intensive manufacturing (garments) or enforced EPF/ESI formalisation would reverse it.

indicators.label: Unemployment rate
indicators.drivers: The headline is held low by self-employment and discouraged workers; graduate joblessness runs about 13%, four times the overall rate.
indicators.breaks: A serious youth-jobs push pulls it down; a hiring freeze in a stress year pushes it up.

indicators.label: Top 1% income share
indicators.drivers: On the World Inequality Lab series the share rose from 18.4% in 2004 to 22.6% in 2022-23, its highest since 1922, with a dip in 2019 and 2020. No annual figure is published after 2022-23.
indicators.breaks: A wealth tax or a more progressive income tax would lower it. Without either, the trend since 2004 points upward.

indicators.label: CPI inflation
indicators.drivers: Food is 36.75% of the CPI basket on the 2024 base (45.86% on the old 2012 base), and about half of cultivated area is rainfed, so inflation still tracks the monsoon.
indicators.breaks: A deficient monsoon or an oil spike pushes CPI above the RBI's 6% ceiling.

indicators.label: Fiscal deficit
indicators.drivers: Consolidation leans on a record RBI dividend and off-budget borrowing.
indicators.breaks: A growth slowdown, a smaller RBI surplus, or new cash-transfer commitments widen it.

indicators.label: Rupee (INR per USD)
indicators.drivers: A $333bn goods deficit is offset by services; FPI outflows and a $123bn oil bill pressure the rupee.
indicators.breaks: An oil shock or sustained FPI exit accelerates depreciation; reserves can only slow it.

indicators.label: Democratic Quality Index
indicators.drivers: It is the geometric mean of the V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index, the Freedom House score, the RSF press-freedom rank and the V-Dem Core Civil Society Index, and all four have worsened since 2014.
indicators.breaks: Restored statistical and press independence would lift it; continued pressure pushes it lower.

bigPicture.note: India in five numbers (IMF World Economic Outlook, April 2026; MoSPI; UN population estimate). The economy is large in total and modest per person.

items.label: Union tax-to-GDP
items.sub: Union gross tax, 2026-27 BE; OECD's ~34% counts all levels of government

chinaDivergence.note: Nominal USD per capita. In 1991 India was at $303 and China at $333 (World Bank). 2026 values are IMF World Economic Outlook (April 2026) projections; 2000-2020 are approximate World Bank values.

taxTake.note: For every ₹100 the Union government receives (Union Budget 2026-27, Budget at a Glance, 'rupee comes from'; rounded). 'shared' flags revenue shared with states via the Finance Commission formula.

items.label: Corporation tax
items.sub: base rate cut from 30% to 22% in 2019

items.label: GST and other taxes
items.sub: falls on everyone at the same rate

spendSplit.note: For every ₹100 the Union government spends (Union Budget 2026-27, Budget at a Glance, 'rupee goes to'). Interest + states' share take 42 paise before a single scheme is funded.

stateReturns.note: Return per ₹100 of taxes paid to the Union, by state, as estimated by Praveen Chakravarty for the All India Professionals' Congress (AIPC). These are the AIPC's own estimates. The Finance Commission publishes no such ratio, and this project has not traced the table behind them, so treat the direction as the finding and the exact ratios as unverified. Rich states finance poorer states, and the system is designed to work that way.

realInflation.note: Your real inflation index: everyday prices over roughly a decade against the 4.8% headline CPI for August 2026 (MoSPI, 2024=100 series). Thali prices: Praveen Chakravarty / AIPC; others illustrative for a mid-market urban household.

external.note: External sector FY26 (RBI Balance of Payments releases for 2025-26; DGCI&S; PPAC; IMF WEO 2026). Goods trade is in deficit, and the services surplus offsets much of it. The current account deficit for 2025-26 was 0.6% of GDP.

distribution.note: Monthly income and where it places you (WIR 2022/2026; HCES 2023-24; PLFS; NCAER). Thresholds approximate. The salaried, tax-paying middle is ~80-120 million, against the 300-400 million quoted by market research. MPCE is HCES 2023-24 without imputation, a mean.

thresholds.label: Bottom 20-25%
thresholds.sub: below rural minimum wage in most states

thresholds.label: Top 3-5%
thresholds.sub: what marketing calls aspirational middle class

structure.note: Output and jobs sit in different sectors (MoSPI GVA at current prices, 2024-25; PLFS employment shares). 'Other' is mining, utilities and construction. Agriculture makes under a fifth of output but holds over two-fifths of jobs.

jobsLesson.note: The same investment creates very different numbers of jobs in different sectors (Praveen Chakravarty / AIPC; Planning Commission 2011-12; garment export-to-jobs ratio industry standard).

indexExample.note: A worked example: an index is one number summarising many prices, via a chosen basket and weights. Change the basket or the base year and the headline moves (MoSPI methodology).

gdpRevision.note: The 2015 GDP revision is still disputed (NSO/MoSPI; A. Subramanian, Harvard CID 2019; EAC-PM rebuttal June 2019).
changes: Manufacturing measured via the MCA21 corporate-filings database instead of the production survey.
Output valued at market prices instead of factor cost.

taxReversal.note: The tax reversal (Union Budget documents; Finance Ministry; PRS; Bharti, Chancel, Piketty and Somanchi, 'Proposals for a Wealth Tax Package to Tackle Extreme Inequalities in India', WIL, May 2024). taxToGDP is the Union's gross tax revenue (2026-27 BE); the OECD average covers all levels of government.

budgetArithmetic.note: BE, RE and actuals (PRS; Union Budget documents). MGNREGA is demand-driven, and its spending has exceeded the budget estimate in every year since 2020-21 (PRS).

kmut.note: Tamil Nadu's KMUT cash transfer (TN Dept of Civil Supplies; KMUT data 2026).

deficitFinancing.note: How the deficit is financed (Union Budget 2026-27; RBI Annual Report 2025-26; PRS).

delimitation.note: Counting people allocates power. Projected Lok Sabha seat change after the first census post-2026 (Carnegie Endowment; ISAS; India Forum). Estimates vary.

monsoonChain.note: Why the monsoon moves inflation (IMD; RBI; NSSO; IPCC). About half of cultivated area is rainfed.

cpiBasket.note: How the CPI number is built. Updated to the CPI 2024=100 series (first published 12 Feb 2026), whose weights come from HCES 2023-24 and which adopts the COICOP 2018 classification in place of the old six-group structure. Food's weight fell from 45.86% under 2012=100 to 36.75% here. This is the single biggest change, and it is the reason headline CPI now moves less on a food-price shock than the pre-2026 series did.

pumpPrice.note: Where the petrol price goes, as an illustration at the excise rate in force before April 2025 (₹19.90 a litre). Tax took about 37 rupees of every hundred. Excise was raised by ₹2 a litre in April 2025 and cut on 27 March 2026, and the Delhi pump price was ₹98.64 from 19 May 2026, so the current split differs (PPAC; PRS; Ministry of Finance notifications).

modiAsks.note: A prime minister asking citizens not to buy gold is a sign of pressure on the balance of payments (PM speech, Hyderabad, 10 May 2026; IMF WEO 2026; RBI/DGCI&S; PPAC).
asks: Avoid buying gold for one year

numbers.label: Gold imports FY26
numbers.sub: largest single commodity import after crude

gold.note: Indians buy gold because the formal system left them no better option (World Gold Council 2024; Commerce Ministry 2025-26 gold import unit value; World Bank Global Findex 2021; IRDAI Annual Report 2024-25; NSE). stockValueTn values 25,000 tonnes at the 2025-26 average import price of about $99,800 a kg. excludedAdultsMn is adults without an account (Findex 2021). equityParticipationPct is NSE's 13.1 crore unique registered investors (May 2026) as a share of population.

poverty.note: Poverty is a contested number. Three official lines give three different answers. India has had no officially accepted poverty line since 2014.

bodies.note: The economy's effects show in health and education outcomes (NFHS-5 2019-21; National Health Accounts; Economic Survey).

readChecklist.note: How to read any official number.
questions: Which definition is being used, and who set it?
What does the number leave out?
When was the underlying data collected?
Who gains if the number looks good?
Did the inconvenient survey get published?
How does it compare with independent estimates?

measurement.note: How we know: four places where a choice of method moved the number more than the economy did (NSO; HCES 2022-23 and 2023-24; Census of India; Carnegie Endowment).

items.title: The GDP back-series
items.body: The 2015 shift to the 2011-12 base and the MCA21 corporate database raised measured growth for the years it covered (2013-14 went from 4.7% to 6.9%). The back-series released in November 2018 then lowered UPA-era growth. Arvind Subramanian (2019) argued that growth in 2011-17 was overstated by about 2.5 points a year.

items.title: The surveys that went missing
items.body: The 2017-18 consumption survey was conducted then withheld (it showed rural consumption falling). That left an 11-year data gap until HCES 2022-23, which changed methodology and is not cleanly comparable.

items.title: A census a decade late
items.body: Last census 2011; the 2021 census was postponed. Census 2027 budget (₹11,718 cr) approved. Welfare ran for a decade on 2011 population numbers.

items.title: Counting = allocating power
items.body: Seats frozen on 1971 data since 1976; the freeze ends with the first census after 2026. Populous northern states gain seats, southern states lose.

states.note: Per-capita NSDP 2023-24 at current prices, 2011-12 series (MoSPI state accounts via api.mospi.gov.in, retrieved 10 October 2026; Haryana, which that table does not carry, from the Economic Survey 2023-24 Statistical Appendix Table 1.11A, as on 15 March 2024); current Lok Sabha seats (543-seat distribution frozen on the 1971 census); population as on 1 March 2026 from the National Commission on Population, 'Population Projections for India and States 2011-2036' (Report of the Technical Group on Population Projections, Registrar General of India), Table 21, converted from thousands to crore; 2011 Census population shown alongside for the comparison; total fertility rate (NFHS-5, 2019-21). 16 states covering about 90% of India's projected 2026 population and 477 of 543 Lok Sabha seats.
states.retNote: Return per ₹100 of Union taxes paid, from Finance Commission devolution, as estimated by Praveen Chakravarty for the All India Professionals' Congress. Available for 8 of the 16 states. This project's author holds an AIPC fellowship, so this is a politically affiliated source on a politically contested question and is flagged as such: treat the direction as well established and the exact ratios as the AIPC's own estimates, which this project has not been able to trace to a published table. Rich states financing poorer ones is how the system is designed to work.
states.delimNote: Projected Lok Sabha seat change after the first census held post-2026 (Carnegie Endowment; ISAS; The India Forum). Available for 4 of the 16 states, and estimates vary considerably between them.
states.popNote: Representation here is computed on the official 2026 projection. The 2011 census is fifteen years stale and would understate how unequal representation has become. The projection is the government's own and is the best available number, but it is a projection because the 2021 census was postponed and the next enumeration is not due until February 2027. A census would replace it with a count. This project's argument applies here as well, because even measuring the fairness of a vote now depends on an estimate.

syntheticControl.note: Independent corroboration from outside this project. Grier & Grier (2026) build a 'Synthetic India', a weighted blend of comparator countries fitted to India's pre-2014 path, and measure the gap that opens after 2014. They are different authors using a different method and a different data vintage, and they reach a convergent conclusion. All values below are transcribed from the authors' published summary; none is recomputed here.

study.title: Promises, Promises: Governance and Growth in India under Modi and the BJP

income.note: The authors publish the first-year and final-year gaps and the pre-treatment fit statistic. They do not publish a machine-readable annual series. Only those published anchor values are stored here; no intermediate years are interpolated or reconstructed.

convergence.grier: Polyarchy gap -0.391, equal to -60.2% of India's 2013 level
Liberal-democracy gap -0.360, equal to -69.1% of India's 2013 level
Freedom-of-expression gap -0.488, equal to -56.2% of India's 2013 level
Political-corruption gap +0.272, equal to +46.8% of India's 2013 level (worse)
convergence.sp: Not separately indexed; SSI covers statistical opacity

syntheticControl.divergence: The two projects agree on direction and differ on scope. Grier & Grier make an absolute income claim, that India ended roughly $1,000 per person per year below its counterfactual, which this project does not test. The authors report that gap as larger than every placebo (p = 0.00) in three of the first four years and larger than all but one (p = 0.08) in the other seven. Some Perspective documents the decoupling of growth from employment and the concentration of its gains, but makes no claim that aggregate income would have been higher under a different government. Their income donor pool is also heavily weighted to Ethiopia (38%) and Bangladesh (25%), a defensible fit to India's pre-2014 trajectory but the part of the design most exposed to challenge. Treat the governance findings as the strongly corroborated result and the income finding as a separate, contestable claim.

eraHistory.note: UPA-decade (2004-2013) values, on the same basis as the 2014+ series so the splice is consistent. Sources: GDP growth and CPI inflation from the World Bank (the same continuous World Bank series used for 2014+); fiscal deficit from the Union Budget/RBI (centre, % GDP); top 1% and bottom 50% income share from the World Inequality Lab (Bharti, Chancel, Piketty and Somanchi 2024, Statistical Appendix), published for 2004-2022; press-freedom rank from RSF. SSI, FCI and DQI before 2014 are computed by the same method as the later years: the SSI from the documented record of survey timeliness, the FCI from published Finance Commission, Union Budget and RBI fiscal series, and the DQI from published V-Dem, Freedom House and RSF scores. See Methodology. Unemployment and formal/informal employment are not extended before 2014, because no annual series on the PLFS basis exists for the UPA decade. Unemployment is shown from 2014, and formal and informal employment for the PLFS survey years 2017-18 to 2023-24.

careEconomy.note: India's two Time Use Surveys, conducted by the National Statistical Office over Jan-Dec 2019 and Jan-Dec 2024. The 2024 round covered 1,39,487 households and 4,54,192 persons aged 6 and over. Unpaid domestic services (minutes and participation) are for persons aged 6 and over; women aged 15-59 who did such work spent 315 minutes a day on it in 2019 and 305 in 2024. Employment participation and caregiving are for ages 15-59. 'Minutes' are the daily average among those who participated in the activity. They are not averages across everyone.
careEconomy.source: NSO Time Use Survey 2019 and 2024, Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (press release, 25 February 2025).

valuations.note: ₹22.7 lakh crore. The most conservative published figure.

valuations.source: Ministry of Women and Child Development (2024 submission)

valuations.note: ₹49.5 lakh crore. Values an hour at what the person could have earned instead.
₹65.1 lakh crore. Values an hour at what it would cost to hire someone to do it.
